title: US Mandates Biometric Photos for All Green Card and Visa Holders at Borders
excerpt: A sweeping DHS rule effective December 2025 requires facial recognition scans of every non-U.S. citizen entering or leaving the country, eliminating previous age exemptions and expanding surveillance to all ports of entry.
body:
• All non-U.S. citizens — including green card holders, visa holders, and children — must now be photographed at every U.S. entry and exit point under a DHS rule effective December 26, 2025.
  • Previous exemptions for travelers under 14 and over 79 have been eliminated; biometric photos may be stored for up to 75 years.
  • CBP plans to roll out the system at all commercial airports and seaports within three to five years, with land border crossings included.

What Changed

The Department of Homeland Security finalized a rule on November 27, 2025, requiring U.S. Customs and Border Protection to photograph all non-U.S. citizens when they enter or leave the United States. The rule, codified in 8 C.F.R. §§ 215 and 235, took effect on December 26, 2025.

CBP had collected fingerprints and photos from certain foreign travelers at select locations since 2004. The new regulation expands this to a comprehensive, mandatory system covering airports, seaports, and land border crossings — with no exceptions for age or visa type.

"Implementing an integrated biometric entry-exit system helps address national security concerns arising from the threat of terrorism and the fraudulent use of legitimate travel documentation."

— U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Federal Register filing

Under the system, CBP uses facial comparison technology to match a live photograph of the traveler against a gallery of facial image templates drawn from passports, visa applications, and prior border encounters. The agency considers this the most accurate, efficient, and least intrusive verification method available.

Who Is Affected

The rule applies to every non-U.S. citizen, regardless of immigration status. Green card holders, H-1B workers, F-1 students, B-1/B-2 visitors, and all other visa categories are covered. Children under 14 and adults over 79 — both previously exempt from biometric collection — are now included.

Photographs taken under the program may be retained by DHS for up to 75 years. CBP has also reserved authority to collect additional biometrics, such as fingerprints, when facial recognition fails or additional verification is needed.

Failure to comply with the photograph requirement can result in a determination of inadmissibility or a finding that the traveler has violated the terms of their immigration status, according to the Gibney Anthony & Flaherty law firm's analysis of the rule.

Implementation Timeline

CBP already operates facial recognition at many major U.S. airports through its "Simplified Arrival" program. The new rule extends mandatory biometric scanning to departures — a gap that previously made it difficult to track visa overstays.

The agency expects to have the system fully operational at all commercial airports and seaports within three to five years, with land border crossings integrated on a rolling basis. Major airports are being prioritized for the initial rollout.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

For the roughly 4.8 million Indian-origin residents in the United States — many on H-1B visas, student visas, or green cards — the rule creates a permanent digital travel record tied to every border crossing.

Immigration attorney Richard T. Herman of the Herman Legal Group warned that the changes carry particular weight for long-term residents. "When travel and status decisions are layered with biometric surveillance, the entire migration ecosystem shifts — including for people who thought their green card gave them stability," he said.

Green card holders who travel frequently to India face heightened scrutiny. Extended absences — now digitally logged at departure — could be used to question continuous U.S. residence, a requirement for maintaining permanent resident status. Multiple long trips abroad may trigger secondary inspection or abandonment inquiries upon return.

Civil rights organizations have flagged concerns about algorithmic bias in facial recognition systems, citing studies showing higher false-positive rates for people with darker skin tones, women, and children. A misidentification could delay boarding or trigger an inspection that complicates future immigration filings.

Privacy and Legal Concerns

The 75-year data retention period and potential sharing of biometric records across federal agencies have drawn criticism from privacy advocates. The rule aligns with a global trend toward biometric border management — the European Union's Entry/Exit System became fully operational across Schengen borders in April 2026 — but the U.S. version goes further by including lawful permanent residents.

"Citizenship isn't just symbolic anymore. It's the legal firewall between routine travel and constant surveillance."

— Richard T. Herman, Herman Legal Group

DHS cites statutory authority under the Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act of 2002, which mandated the creation of a biometric entry-exit system following the September 11 attacks. The rule represents the permanent implementation of what had been a decades-long series of pilot programs.

What Travelers Should Do

Immigration attorneys recommend that affected travelers carry original immigration documents — passport, visa, I-94, and green card — and allow extra time for biometric processing at departure and arrival. Green card holders spending extended periods abroad should maintain evidence of U.S. ties, including tax filings, lease agreements, and employment records.

Some legal experts have advised long-term permanent residents to consider naturalization as a way to avoid ongoing biometric exit tracking, since U.S. citizens are exempt from the departure photography requirement.
nri_angle: Indian green card and visa holders face permanent biometric tracking at U.S. borders, with implications for frequent India travelers and continuous residence requirements.
